caveats: This is a small hand-authored semantic transfer smoke, not a statistical benchmark.
Rows with source=definition_anchored_hand_authored are not quoted source text; they are canonical semantic fixtures built from the authoritative TKS/CAS noetic definitions.
Strong performance here would support transfer to original-TKS-style examples, but does not by itself prove mechanistic encoding.

layer3_predictions.english: Get a dog to sit on command.
The dog is paying attention to the trainer's commands, processing and entertaining the idea.
The trainer uses a dog treat to lure and reward the dog with something the dog likes.
A historical aversive correction gives the dog something it dislikes when it fails to follow the command.
The dog's gradual acceptance of the command is judged by how long it stays sitting and how quickly it responds.
The dog's mind is composed of temperament and training tendencies inherited through pedigree.

The idea of sitting on command contains nested sub-ideas such as the verbal cue, posture, reward expectation, trainer relationship, and repeated practice, while also belonging to the larger training system.
The dog's training schedule and the length of training sessions set the repeated pattern of exposure to the command.
The trainer's verbal command sit acts as a trigger that brings a different idea to the dog's mind.
An image of the dog treat enters the dog's mind after the triggering command.
The policy position itself is the object under discussion.
The debater holds the opponent's claim in attention long enough to understand it.
One piece of evidence appeals to the debater as the strongest support for the case.
A weak source feels unsuitable, and the debater pushes it out of the argument.
A statistic leaves a strong impression and keeps echoing in the debater's mind.
The debater's values and past experience shape what arguments feel natural to make.
The final argument is built from a claim, evidence, warrant, objection, and reply.
Repeated timed practice rounds set the pattern by which the debater meets the material.
The opponent's question acts as a trigger that points the debater toward a stored case.
The counterpoint arrives in the debater's mind as the answer to that trigger.
The missing keys are the object the search is about.
The person searches memory and attends to the last moments before entering the house.
The familiar bowl by the door draws attention as the most likely place to check first.
The idea that the keys fell outside feels wrong, so the person resists that possibility.
The memory of a metal sound on the counter leaves a strong impression.
The person's habits and household routines shape the search before any new clue appears.
The search plan is made of smaller parts: rooms, pockets, bags, counters, and last actions.
Every day the same sequence repeats: unlock the door, step inside, set things down.
Seeing the jacket on the chair triggers the memory of reaching into its pocket.
The thought of the coat pocket appears as the remembered place to check.
The bug report is the object the developer is trying to understand.
The developer focuses on the failing test and keeps the relevant inputs in awareness.
A stack trace stands out as promising and pulls the developer toward one file.
The explanation involving a flaky network call feels wrong and gets pushed aside.
The repeated error message makes a strong impression because it appears every run.
The developer's years of parser bugs shape what possibilities feel familiar.
The bug hypothesis is made of logs, input shape, parser state, and the line that changed.
The developer reruns the same test after each edit, building a repeated check cycle.
The failing assertion triggers suspicion about an off-by-one boundary.
The off-by-one possibility appears as the next thing to inspect.
The painting is the object before the viewer.
The viewer studies the brushwork and holds the image in awareness.
A warm patch of color attracts the viewer and keeps pulling the gaze back.
A harsh figure in the corner repels the viewer and feels difficult to look at.
The whole image leaves a lasting impression after the viewer walks away.
The viewer's memories of home shape what the painting seems to mean.
The painting's theme is made from smaller parts: light, figure, background, color, and gesture.
Each return to the same gallery wall changes the viewer through repeated exposure.
The painted doorway triggers a memory of the viewer's childhood house.
The childhood-house memory appears in the viewer's mind after seeing the doorway.
